newsitem.title: UK: Hardline Unionist riled by Blair's IRA talks plan.
newsitem.headline: Hardline Unionist riled by Blair's IRA talks plan.

text.p: A senior Protestant politician on Thursday brusquely rejected British terms for giving IRA guerrillas a political voice in Northern Ireland peace talks.

A day after Prime Minister Tony Blair launched a bid to to revive the stalled peace process, Peter Robinson warned that his Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) would walk out if the Irish Republican Army's political arm Sinn Fein was given a seat at peace talks six weeks after a fresh IRA truce.
But other political parties welcomed parts of a wide-ranging Blair initiative framed jointly with Dublin -- Protestant Unionists cautiously and Catholic nationalists enthusiastically.

The initiative comprised Anglo-Irish proposals for disarming guerrillas, a September target for starting full scale Northern Ireland talks and a British offer that Sinn Fein could be in talks six weeks after an unequivocal IRA truce.
Irish newspapers praised what they said was Blair's obvious commitment to peace since he came to office, replacing John Major, in a May 1 election landslide.
Political commentators however ruled out a quick truce by the IRA in its fight to end British rule in Northern Ireland.

They said the guerrillas, who style themselves defenders of the minority Catholics, would wait to see how Britain dealt with a series of contentious parades by pro-British Protestants that have sparked fears of widespread trouble.
Robinson, echoing charges by DUP leader Ian Paisley that Britain was appeasing the IRA and Sinn Fein, said six weeks was too short to assess whether any new guerrilla truce was not a sham.
"If Sinn Fein are in the process at a time when it is impossible for them to be judged to have been genuine, we will not be there," Robinson, deputy leader of the DUP, told BBC radio.

The DUP is a pro-British party with history of hardline opposition to Anglo-Irish policies. The main party of the majority Protestants, the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), said parts of the arms decommissioning package were seriously deficient but, significantly, the party did not reject it.
UUP spokesman Ken Maginnis said on BBC radio the government's commitment to total disarmament of all guerrillas was a sign of progress.
London and Dublin hope the UUP and the main Catholic Social Democratic and Labour Party will be able to make rare progress in talks, in the face of DUP objections.
The arms decommissioning proposals were framed to win a new IRA truce and ensure that, with or without Sinn Fein participation, negotiations would proceed.

David Davin-Power, Northern Ireland editor for RTE, Ireland's broadcasting network, said he did not think the IRA would rush into calling off violence, but would await the outcome of the "marching season" and clarification of the decommissioning plans currently being sought by Sinn Fein.
"We are unlikely to see a ceasefire before mid-July at the very earliest, and probably not until August -- if it is going to happen," he told Reuters.
Blair said his six-week offer had been transmitted to Sinn Fein three days before the IRA shot dead two Northern Ireland policemen on June 16.
Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams gave a guarded welcome to the plans but said he wanted to know preceisely how Britain will ensure that the arms row will not continue to dog negotiations.
